soil-bio-198.title: The root cap, a helmet that steers the root
soil-bio-198.text: Every growing root pushes through soil behind a small shield. The root cap, or calyptra, covers the tip of each growing root. It protects the apical meristem, the zone of dividing cells, and eases the root's passage. It also steers. Statoliths, dense grains, settle in its gravity-sensing statocytes and drive gravitropism, growth in response to gravity. Remove the cap and the root grows at random. It secretes a mucilage layer that cuts friction and may foster signaling with soil microbes. The cap renews itself as its oldest outer layers slough off, in cereals and many legumes as long-lived border cells.

soil-bio-202.title: Endophytes, the microbes living quietly inside plants
soil-bio-202.text: Every plant species studied so far carries hidden tenants. An endophyte is a microbe, often a bacterium or fungus, that lives inside a plant for at least part of its life without causing apparent disease. Most of these relationships are still poorly understood. Some pass from parent to offspring through seeds, called vertical transmission. Others spread between plants by spores, called horizontal transmission. Many are mutualists. They help hosts cope with pathogens, drought, heat, poor soils, salinity and grazing animals, and they receive carbon in return. They can raise uptake of scarce soil elements such as phosphorus and make rock phosphate and atmospheric nitrogen available to the plant. Systemic endophytes stay harmless for the plant's whole life. Non-systemic ones vary with conditions and can turn pathogenic when the host is stressed. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi are one group of fungal endophytes, while bacterial endophytes come from many unrelated groups. Fungicides harm endophytic fungi, and fertilizers lessen a plant's reliance on them. Epichloë endophytes are used commercially in turf grasses.

soil-bio-200.title: Frankia, the nitrogen fixer once mistaken for a fungus
soil-bio-200.text: In 1886 Brunchorst named the genus Frankia, taking it for a fungus. In 1970 Becking redefined it as a prokaryotic actinomycete. These filamentous bacteria fix nitrogen in the root nodules of actinorhizal plants, much as {{ref:soil-bio-178}} do in legumes. With a special enzyme they turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, often meeting most or all of the host's needs, so hosts thrive in poor soils. Most strains are host-specific. Hosts include all alders, some Casuarina species, sea-buckthorn, Myrica and Ceanothus. Infection runs through deformed root hairs or between root cells, and a nodule primordium forms.

soil-bio-201.title: Nod factors, the signal that tells a legume to build a nodule
soil-bio-201.text: A legume and its bacteria agree to build a nodule by trading chemical messages. Plant flavonoids activate the bacterial regulator NodD, which switches on the nod genes. These make Nod factors, the signals that trigger root nodule formation. They are lipochitooligosaccharides: chains of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine carrying a fatty acid, with strain-specific additions. Receptors called NFR1 and NFR5, first isolated in Lotus japonicus in 2003, perceive them. Calcium floods in and early nodulin genes start. The root hair curls round the bacteria, and an infection thread carries them inward to where they fix nitrogen as bacteroids.

soil-bio-199.title: Pneumatophores, roots that rise to breathe
soil-bio-199.text: Oxygen diffuses four orders of magnitude faster in air than in water. In waterlogged soil, roots starve for it. Pneumatophores are specialized aerial roots that let plants breathe there. They grow down from the stem or up from ordinary roots. Porous lenticels lead into air-filled aerenchyma, spongy tissue that helps gases spread through the plant. Black and grey mangroves bear them, and mangrove aerial roots serve aeration rather than water uptake. Cypress knees were once thought to be pneumatophores. But they lack aerenchyma and exchange little gas, and their function remains unclear.
